course: CMU 21-254: Linear Algebra and Vector Calculus for Engineers
audience: SI leader teaching live on a whiteboard. This is not a student worksheet.
toneRule: Keep explanations very simple, verbal, and board-friendly. Avoid textbook phrasing unless the problem needs it.
title: Diagonalization and Matrix Powers
sessionGoal: Students should be able to write A = PDP⁻¹ when enough eigenvectors exist and use it to compute powers efficiently.
quickStartIfUnprepared: Start with the sentence: diagonalization changes to an eigenvector coordinate system.
Do Problem 1 as the main full diagonalization example.
If time is short, skip the symbolic formula and compute A^3 only.
Use Problem 2 to show powers acting on a vector without multiplying matrices repeatedly.
sayThisFirst: The columns of P are eigenvectors.
The diagonal entries of D are the matching eigenvalues in the same order.
Matrix powers become easier because A^n=PD^nP^{-1}.
boardPlan: Write the diagonalization recipe: eigenvalues, eigenvectors, build P and D.
Emphasize matching order: column 1 of P matches entry 1 of D.
Use D^n to compute a power.
Do the vector power problem if time remains.
keyFormulas: D = diagonal matrix of matching eigenvalues.
A is diagonalizable when it has enough independent eigenvectors.
commonMistakes: Putting eigenvalues in D in an order that does not match P.
Using A^n=P D (P^{-1})^n instead of A^n=P D^n P^{-1}.
notationWarnings: If \(P=[\,v_1\ \ v_2\,]\), then \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\) in that same order.
Use A^n=PD^nP^{-1}; the P and P^{-1} do not get powers.

problems.title: Diagonalize a 2 by 2 matrix and compute \(A^3\)
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \[A=\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{bmatrix}.\] Use the eigenvectors \(v_1=(2,1)\) for \(\lambda_1=5\) and \(v_2=(1,-1)\) for \(\lambda_2=2\) to diagonalize \(A\). Then compute \(A^3\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: the eigenvectors and eigenvalues are already given, so the main issue is organizing P and D correctly.

drawInstructions: Draw A as complicated in standard coordinates.
Draw P^{-1} as changing into eigenvector coordinates.
Draw D as simple stretching by 5 and 2.

walkthrough.label: Build P and D in matching order

commonMistakes: Putting the eigenvectors as rows of P instead of columns.
Putting 2 before 5 in D while leaving P unchanged.
Computing A^3 by multiplying A three times even though diagonalization is available.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 6 for diagonalization and powers.

problems.title: Use eigenvectors to compute \(A^nx\)
problems.studentPromptLatex: Suppose \(A v_1=3v_1\) for \(v_1=(1,1)\), and \(A v_2=-v_2\) for \(v_2=(1,-1)\). Let \(x=(5,1)\). Find a formula for \(A^n x\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: write x in the eigenvector basis. Then powers just power the eigenvalues.

drawInstructions: Draw x as a combination of the two eigenvector directions.
Label: the \(v_1\) component gets multiplied by \(3^n\).
Label: the \(v_2\) component gets multiplied by \((-1)^n\).

walkthrough.label: Write x as a combination of eigenvectors
Solve for the coefficients
walkthrough.latex: This gives \(c_1+c_2=5\) and \(c_1-c_2=1\). Adding gives \(2c_1=6\), so \(c_1=3\). Then \(c_2=2\).

walkthrough.label: Apply A^n to each eigenvector piece
walkthrough.latex: \[A^n x=A^n(3v_1+2v_2)=3A^n v_1+2A^n v_2.\] Each piece picks up its eigenvalue: \(A^n v_1=3^n v_1\) and \(A^n v_2=(-1)^n v_2\).

commonMistakes: Trying to find A explicitly even though it is not needed.
Forgetting to decompose x into eigenvectors first.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 6 for powers using diagonalization.

problems.title: Diagonalize a triangular matrix with distinct eigenvalues
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \[C=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&2&1\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}.\] Diagonalize \(C\) by finding matrices \(P\) and \(D\) such that \(C=PDP^{-1}\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: distinct eigenvalues usually make diagonalization straightforward, but we still need eigenvectors.

drawInstructions: Circle the diagonal entries to get eigenvalues.
Write one eigenvector under each eigenvalue.
Build P with those eigenvectors as columns.

walkthrough.label: Find eigenvalues
walkthrough.latex: The matrix is triangular, so the eigenvalues are \(1,2,3\).

walkthrough.label: Find eigenvector for λ=1
walkthrough.latex: \[C-I=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&2\end{bmatrix}.\] This gives \(z=0\) and \(y=0\), so one eigenvector is \((1,0,0)\).

walkthrough.label: Find eigenvector for λ=2
walkthrough.latex: \[C-2I=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}.\] This gives \(x=0\), \(z=0\), with \(y\) free. One eigenvector is \((0,1,0)\).

walkthrough.label: Find eigenvector for λ=3
walkthrough.latex: \[C-3I=\begin{bmatrix}-2&0&0\\0&-1&1\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}.\] This gives \(x=0\) and \(-y+z=0\), so \(z=y\). One eigenvector is \((0,1,1)\).

walkthrough.label: Build P and D
walkthrough.latex: Use the eigenvectors in the same order as the eigenvalues: \[P=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad D=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}.\]

commonMistakes: Reading eigenvalues correctly but skipping eigenvectors.
Putting eigenvectors in P in a different order than D.
Assuming D is the original diagonal of C and forgetting P.

wrapUpQuestions: Why is D^n easy to compute?
What order mistake breaks the diagonalization?

reviewSummary: Session 13 turns eigenvectors into a practical tool for powers.

open.title: Change coordinates, and the matrix becomes easy
say: Last time we asked: are there enough eigenvectors? Today's payoff: when there are, the matrix becomes a diagonal matrix in disguise.
Diagonal matrices are the easiest matrices in the world. Multiplying them, powering them, reading them: all easy. Diagonalization lets us borrow that ease for any matrix with an eigenbasis.

ask.a: The diagonal matrix with entries 2¹⁰ and 3¹⁰. Just power the diagonal.

idea.title: Translate, stretch, translate back
say: Read PDP⁻¹ from right to left. P⁻¹ translates a vector into eigenvector coordinates. D stretches each coordinate by its eigenvalue. P translates back to standard coordinates.
Powers are where this pays off. In A·A·A, every P⁻¹P in the middle cancels, so A³ = PD³P⁻¹. The hard part, powering, happens only to D.
The one rule you cannot break: column j of P and entry j of D belong to the same eigenpair.
draw: Draw three boxes in a row: 'standard coords' → P⁻¹ → 'eigen coords' → D (stretch) → 'eigen coords' → P → 'standard coords'.
Under it write A·A·A = PDP⁻¹ · PDP⁻¹ · PDP⁻¹ and cross out each P⁻¹P pair.
Draw P and D side by side with an arrow from column 1 of P to the first diagonal entry of D.

ask.q: Why do the middle P⁻¹P pairs cancel?
ask.a: P⁻¹P = I, so they multiply to nothing.

ask.q: If you swap the columns of P, what else must you do?
ask.a: Swap the diagonal entries of D the same way.

launch.say: The eigenpairs are given. Build P and D, find P⁻¹, then compute A³ the fast way.
circulate: Check the columns of P match the order of D.
Watch the P⁻¹ formula: divide by det P = −3.
Encourage checking the answer: A² then A³ is only two multiplications for a 2 × 2.

askFirst.q: Before computing: check that v₁ really is an eigenvector.

steps.say: v₁ goes first in P, so its eigenvalue 5 goes first in D.

ask.q: Eigenvectors: rows or columns of P?

steps.why: AP = PD says exactly 'A times each column of P equals that column times its eigenvalue'.

steps.say: det P = −2 − 1 = −3. Swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by −3.

ask.a: P times it should be I. First row: 2/3 + 1/3 = 1 and 2/3 − 2/3 = 0. ✓

steps.say: D³ just cubes the diagonal: diag(125, 8). So A³ = PD³P⁻¹.

ask.a: P · diag(5¹⁰⁰, 2¹⁰⁰) · P⁻¹. Same amount of work as A³.

steps.say: Multiply left to right: first PD³, then multiply that by P⁻¹. One entry at a time.

ask.q: How can you check this without trusting the diagonalization?
ask.a: A² has rows (18, 14) and (7, 11), and A² · A gives the same matrix. ✓

si13-p1.meaning: A stretches the (2, 1) direction by 5 and the (1, −1) direction by 2. Applying A three times stretches them by 125 and 8. Everything else is just translating in and out of those directions.

ifStuck.if: a student gets fractions that don't simplify to integers
ifStuck.then: check P⁻¹ first; the most common slip is dividing by +3 instead of −3.

ifStuck.if: a student puts 2 first in D
ifStuck.then: ask which eigenvector is in column 1 of P.

si13-p1.transition: We needed P⁻¹ there. Next: a way to power a matrix on one vector without ever building P⁻¹ or even knowing A.

launch.say: We don't know A. We know two eigenpairs and a vector x. Find a formula for Aⁿx.
circulate: Is anyone trying to reconstruct A? Redirect: split x into eigenvectors.

askFirst.q: What's easy to compute: Aⁿ v₁ or Aⁿ x?
askFirst.a: Aⁿ v₁ = 3ⁿ v₁. So we want x in terms of v₁ and v₂.

steps.say: Write x = c₁v₁ + c₂v₂: (5, 1) = c₁(1, 1) + c₂(1, −1).

ask.q: Why can we always do this here?
ask.a: v₁ and v₂ are independent, so they form a basis of ℝ².

steps.say: c₁ + c₂ = 5 and c₁ − c₂ = 1. Add: c₁ = 3, so c₂ = 2.
Aⁿ passes through the combination: 3Aⁿv₁ + 2Aⁿv₂, and each piece just gets its eigenvalue to the n.
steps.why: This is the same idea as PDⁿP⁻¹. Finding c₁, c₂ is what P⁻¹ does.

ask.q: For large n, which piece dominates?
ask.a: The 3ⁿ piece; the other just flips sign. Aⁿx points more and more along (1, 1).

si13-p2.meaning: Each application of A triples the (1, 1) part of x and flips the (1, −1) part. After many steps, x lines up with the dominant eigenvector (1, 1).

ifStuck.then: compute A²x together; the eigenvalue gets applied twice, so it's 3², not 3 · 2.

si13-p2.transition: Last one: a full 3 × 3 diagonalization from scratch, the exam version.

launch.say: Diagonalize C: find P and D.
circulate: Eigenvalues are free (triangular), but each eigenvector still needs a computation.
Check the λ = 3 eigenvector: z = y, not z = −y.

askFirst.q: Distinct eigenvalues 1, 2, 3. Is C guaranteed diagonalizable?
askFirst.a: Yes: three distinct eigenvalues give three independent eigenvectors.

ask.q: What does 'distinct' save us from checking?
ask.a: Whether any GM falls short of its AM.

steps.say: C − I: rows give y + z = 0 and 2z = 0, so y = z = 0. Eigenvector (1, 0, 0).

ask.a: Yes: column 1 of C − I is all zeros.

steps.say: C − 2I: x = 0 and z = 0, with y free. Eigenvector (0, 1, 0).
C − 3I: x = 0 and −y + z = 0, so z = y. Eigenvector (0, 1, 1).
Eigenvectors as columns in the order 1, 2, 3; D = diag(1, 2, 3).

ask.q: Is D just the diagonal of C?
ask.a: Here, yes, the entries match, but C ≠ D. The work was finding P.

steps.why: D alone doesn't diagonalize anything. P is what connects C to D.

si13-p3.meaning: C is a shear-plus-stretch in standard coordinates, but along the directions (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (0, 1, 1) it simply stretches by 1, 2 and 3.

ifStuck.if: a student answers only with D
ifStuck.then: ask them to check C = PDP⁻¹ with P = I. It fails because of the off-diagonal 1.

wrap.write: A = PDP⁻¹: eigenvectors in P, eigenvalues in D, same order. Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹. For Aⁿx, split x into eigenvectors and power each eigenvalue.

exit.q: What goes in P? In D?
exit.a: Eigenvectors as columns; matching eigenvalues on the diagonal.
Reordering D without reordering the columns of P (or vice versa).

wrap.next: Next session: projections and the cross product, splitting a vector into 'along' and 'across' pieces.
